questions.q: According to this lesson, what is more convincing in a portfolio review than a slide deck?
options: A verbal description with no repository to show
A certificate with no accompanying code
A written essay describing Git concepts
A real repository you can walk through directly
questions.explain: Real, working code — a repository someone can actually open and inspect — is more convincing than any description of it.

questions.q: In what order does this lesson recommend walking through the capstone repository?
options: Alphabetically by filename
Only the README file — nothing else needs to be shown
The deploy job first, then work backward with no particular reason
.gitignore, a real pull request, the workflow file, a failed then passing run, then the deploy job
questions.explain: This order builds a narrative — from basic hygiene through review, CI proof, and finally deployment.

questions.q: What should you be able to explain if asked 'what would happen if you accidentally committed a password?'
options: That Git automatically deletes passwords from history
Both the .gitignore prevention and the reality that the credential would still need to be rotated
That it's impossible to accidentally commit a password
That nothing bad would happen since GitHub is private
questions.explain: This callback to Lesson 12 requires knowing both the preventive measure and what's still needed if prevention fails.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what was this course really about, beyond individual Git commands?
options: Catching a change that could break something before it reaches someone who trusted the number
Memorizing as many CLI flags as possible
Passing a certification exam with no practical application
Learning to use exactly one specific CI tool forever
questions.explain: The real throughline is preventing broken changes from silently reaching people who rely on the data — the specific commands are just the mechanism.

questions.q: What does this lesson say transfers to any team, tool, or stack, even though the specific YAML will differ?
options: The specific database vendor used
The instinct to ask whether a change has a test gate before it reaches production
The exact filename of the workflow file
The exact wording of every commit message
questions.explain: The underlying habit — checking for a gate before production — is what generalizes, regardless of the specific tools involved.
